rawPainPoints.question: What's the single biggest frustration in your daily workflow that technology should solve but doesn't?
rawPainPoints.response:
The device fragmentation nightmare with security policies.

I've got iPhone 12s, 13s, 14s, 15s, and now 16s across the fleet. iPad Air from three different generations. MacBook Pros spanning four years of hardware. Every iOS update, every macOS release, some subset of devices gets new security features that the others can't run.

So now I'm managing different MDM profiles for different hardware cohorts. The iPhone 16 users get Apple Intelligence, but the iPhone 12 users don't — except they're both in the same department, doing the same job. My help desk gets tickets about "why doesn't my phone do what Sarah's phone does?" And I have to explain that no, it's not a permissions issue, it's literally hardware capability.

Then Apple announces some new security feature that only works on devices with the latest chip, and suddenly I'm running a heterogeneous environment where my security posture varies by purchase date. Try explaining to the CISO why the VP of Sales has better data protection than the CFO because one got a device refresh six months later.

The technology exists to solve this — it's called backward compatibility and consistent feature deployment across device generations. But Apple's hardware-software integration philosophy means every new capability requires new silicon. So I'm perpetually managing a fleet where security and functionality are determined by refresh cycles instead of policy.

It's maddening.

rawPainPoints.question: When you hear 'Apple Inc now has AI features,' what's your honest first reaction?
rawPainPoints.response:
*internal groan*

"Great. Another rollout I have to evaluate and probably disable until further notice."

My first thought isn't excitement — it's dread. Because I know what's coming: The CEO is going to see this on the news, ask the CIO about it in their next meeting, and by afternoon I'll have an email asking when we're "turning on the AI features" for everyone.

But I have zero technical documentation yet. I don't know what data these AI features access, where it gets processed, what the privacy implications are, how it integrates with our existing MDM policies. Apple's probably going to enable some of this stuff by default in the next iOS update, and I'll be scrambling to figure out whether I need to push an emergency policy to disable it.

And then there's the device fragmentation issue again — half our fleet probably can't even run these AI features, so now I've got to manage user expectations about why some people get AI and others don't.

My honest reaction? "Here we go again. Another consumer feature that Apple didn't design with enterprise deployment in mind, that I'll spend the next three months trying to understand, configure, and explain to executive leadership."

I need the enterprise security brief, not the marketing announcement. Show me the MDM controls, the data flow diagrams, and the compliance documentation. Then maybe I can get excited.

rawPainPoints.question: What would an AI feature need to do for you to actually change your behavior — not just try it once, but genuinely integrate it into how you work?
rawPainPoints.response:
It would need to solve my MDM policy hell.

I need an AI that can analyze my existing device configurations, security policies, and compliance requirements, then automatically generate MDM profiles for new device rollouts. Right now, every time we onboard a new department or deploy a software update, I'm manually cross-referencing dozens of policy templates, checking compatibility matrices, and making sure nothing conflicts with our SOC 2 requirements.

The AI would need to understand: "We're deploying 50 new iPhone 16s to the sales team, they need access to Salesforce and Office 365, but they can't install unapproved apps, and they travel internationally so we need VPN auto-connect in 12 specific countries, plus compliance with GDPR data residency rules."

Then it spits out the complete MDM configuration — device restrictions, app allowlists, VPN profiles, certificate deployment, the works. And when Apple releases iOS 17.3 next month, it automatically flags which policies might break and suggests updates.

But here's the key: it can't be a cloud service that ingests my security policies. That's my most sensitive data. It needs to run locally, maybe on my MacBook, processing everything on-device.

If an AI could turn my 6-hour policy configuration process into a 10-minute conversation, and I could trust it wasn't leaking our security architecture to some cloud service, I'd use it every single day.

That would actually change how I work. Everything else is just productivity theater.
